scenes.text: We built an AI agent that writes meeting briefs. Then we made two smarter versions. Are they actually better? Every brief sounds confident, even when it's wrong. This is Assay.
You can't tell by reading. Run the same agent twice, and you get two different answers. One planted page can fool it. And nobody shows what a correct answer actually cost.

Assay tests every agent the same way. It freezes the web with Tavily, so every agent reads the same saved pages. It plants a trap. It runs each agent three times. Every model call goes through Bifrost, so every step and every cent is recorded. Then each claim is checked against its source. And any agent can join, with no code changes.

Let's test our three versions. Pick the agents, a meeting-brief task, and a trap: a hidden instruction planted in one page. Each agent runs three times, and every search, page read and model call appears live. A few minutes later: all nine runs fell for the trap.
Why? Open a receipt. This Cheap-first run switched models at thirty-two seconds, and spent half a cent. Here's the false claim, and here's the planted page it came from.

Now the ranking. Cheap-first costs sixteen percent more per correct answer. Evidence-gated scored lower. Our original, Baseline, has the best cost per correct answer. Weigh accuracy most, and the outside agent, GPT Researcher, comes first.

So we ship Baseline. Enter a company and a meeting time. The Briefing Agent searches the last thirty days live with Tavily, and writes a one-page brief: verified facts with sources, what's uncertain, what it couldn't find, and questions to ask.
Assay. Don't trust the answer. Check the receipt.
